Perhaps the minister
would make a statement.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
As the committee knows, this is the most important item in the estimates of the Department of Pensions. It covers the payment of pensions to those who were injured during the great war. Pensions are paid to disabled ex-members of the Canadian expeditionary force and their dependants numbering-and I am quoting the figures somewhat inaccurately-something like 253,000 people. Pensions are payable also to members of the active militia who since

Supply-Pensions-European War
August 4, 1914, have incurred disabilities, and to the dependants of those who died in military service. The item also covers the reinstatement of pensioners who have commuted their pensions. It gives gratuities to pensioners who have less than five per cent disability. It also provides for certain supplementary pensions payable to Canadian citizens, that is to say, people who were resident in Canada but who, during the war, served in the British army. It also provides certain additional pensions under certain conditions to ex-members of the Belgian, French and Italian forces. Arrangements have also been made with the Dominion of New Zealand whereby certain members of the New Zealand expeditionary force who are entitled to pension under their own law, whilst residing in Canada receive their allowances or pensions from the Canadian government, which afterwards recovers the amount from the sister dominion. It provides also for burial grants to pensioners who die having no means for the payment of their funeral expenses. And it covers payments to members of the permanent force who have been injured subsequent to August 4, 1914.
It is somewhat hazardous for a minister to make any statement of what the future will bring. I well recollect that some fifteen years ago the then Minister of Pensions stated that the peak of pensions had been reached. At that time the pension bill was something under $20,000,000. To-day I have the honour to ask the committee for $41,-
500,000.	But I have reason to believe that in so far as pensions are concerned-and I wish it to be well understood that I am speaking only of pensions, that is, payments made to those who incurred disability on service- I believe that we have about reached the peak. I may say in passing that there are other expenditures which are being and which will be made on behalf of veterans of the great war that are bound to increase as the years go by. For instance, the war veterans' allowances, which are paid to those who are assumed to have a disability but who cannot establish through the courts which have been set up by our legislation that their disability is due to the war, are now being paid to the extent of $4,200,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is another item in the estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Yes, but I want to make it plain that while I am saying that perhaps the peak of pensions as such has been or is about to be reached, the highest total annual payment made by the people of Canada to
ex-soldiers will not be reached for some years to come. As a matter of fact in war veterans' allowances alone we are asking the committee to grant this year an additional $800,000, and that will gradually mount up until war veterans' allowance payments will reach the total of something like $13,000,000 in, I think, 1957.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: As the minister has mentioned that, would he say how that sum is arrived at? Or he can reserve that until the item itself is up.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
When the War Veterans'
Allowance Act was introduced certain computations were made, and so far they have proven fairly correct. If they continue to operate in the same manner, and there is no further legislation making the provisions more generous, we have reason to hope that by 1957 the total of $13,000,000 for war veterans' allowances will be about the peak.
As far as pensions are concerned, the peak was in 1931-32, when the amount actually expended was $46,795,039.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The number of pensioners has been increasing since then, but the amount expended is less?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The number of pensioners has increased. As a matter of fact in the past six months as compared with last year it has increased by something like 220. The number of pensioners who were actually receiving pension on September 30, 1936, was 97,865, of whom 79,467 were disability pensioners and 18,054 were dependent pensioners.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Including widows and
children.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
And the amount paid to
September of this year was $20,776,000.
The reason for hoping that there will be some diminution is that we believe that as a result of the action of the committee set up last year the applicants who are really entitled to pension will have a greater opportunity of bringing their cases before the tribunal, whereas those who have been what might be called chronic pension chasers will have less opportunity. So that for one thing the expense of administration should decrease. As is well known to the committee, the judicial set-up has through the years become somewhat more complicated than perhaps it should be, and I say that knowing full well that I must bear my own share of the responsibility of having asked for it in this house. Let us hope that within a very short time the arrears of pension cases will be

Supply-Pensions-European War
caught up with. In fact I am informed by the chairman of the pension commission that by March 31 of this year we shall no longer have any arrears of pension cases. That, I think, will lead to considerable economy. Then, as a result of legislation passed in 1933, children born to pensioners after May 1, 1933, I think, are not longer entitled to pension. The number now going off pension is quite considerable. We find, for instance, that in February of 1937 the number who reach the age at which they will no longer be entitled to pension, that is, sixteen years, normally, is 1,029. In all, 11,475 will be cut off pension during 1937.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is included in the
20,000 dependents the hon. gentleman mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Exactly. During 1938 there will be 10,518 cut off; during 1939 there will be 10,189, and from then on the number goes down very rapidly. Then, of course, there is the mortality. The average age of pensioners at the present time is forty-eight years and nine months.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is other than
dependents?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, disability pensioners.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: What does the minister mean when he says they will be cut off after those years?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Under the pension legislation children of pensioners receive an allowance up to the age of sixteen normally, seventeen for girls. Under certain circumstances, if in the discretion of the tribunal it is considered reasonable they are allowed to carry on until the age of twenty-one, but there is no such thing as permanent pension for children of pensioners. Their allowance continues only until such time as they are supposed to have finished their education or until they are assumed to be able to earn a living.
The pensioners themselves are dying off at a fairly rapid rate. I would assume that at the present time there are just about as many pensioners who die off as there are new ones who come on. During the year 1935-36, for instance, there were 1,040 disability pensioners who died, and 553 main dependents. By that I do not mean children; I mean wives. That makes a total of 1,593 who no longer draw pensions on account of their decease. That figure has been rising, not very rapidly but fairly gradually, since 1028, when the figure was 1,014. In 1931-32 it rose to 1,333, and the highest figure is that I have just mentioned, 1,593.

So there is some ground for belief that we have reached the peak in pensions. I want it to be very clearly understood by the committee, however, that this does not mean to say that we have reached the peak of expenditure on behalf of returned soldiers in Canada. As they grow older, as more and more of them come on the war veterans' allowances, under the statute they must be looked after. As more and more become unable to cope with the ordinary competition of civilian life they will have to be looked after, somehow or another. Personally I have never cared to think of opening old soldiers' homes in this country. I do not think the Canadian people want them; I do not think the old soldiers themselves want them, but I am bound to say to the committee that the time will come when some measure or another will have to be taken to look after those who gave good service to the country at the front and who are unable to look after themselves otherwise.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to express
the appreciation of a family in Fort William. A returned man was stricken with an incurable disease and confined to the general hospital in Winnipeg. His parents, who were around eighty years of age, desired to have their son come home and spend this last days in Fort William. I got in touch with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) by mail; he got in touch with the pensions department, and in less than five days this returned man was in the McKellar hospital in Fort William. Since then he has answered the last roll call, and on behalf of his parents I would express to the Minister of Pensions and those assisting him their deep appreciation. I think this shows that this department has some heart, and I hope the department will continue to show it, so that any man who has served overseas may obtain that which will satisfy him when his body and mind are weakening.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
May I ask the minister whether he has yet had a report from the War Veterans' Assistance Commission which was appointed last year? I ask that question for this reason. That commission has travelled across this country and has heard representations of many different kinds. I think several of these items which will come up to-night should stand over until we have had at least an interim report from that commission. The committee on pensions and returned soldiers' problems which sat last year brought in a recommendation in these terms:
To ensure that the progress of the commission's activities, both in connection with its surveys and application of approved projects,

Supply-Pensions-European War
be made known to the government, your committee would also recommend that the commission be required to submit from time to time interim reports on matters arising out of the act.
The act which was passed provided, in section 12:
The minister may from time to time require the commission to submit a report on the progress of projects and other matters arising out of this act, and the commission shall, before the expiry of the term of office of the commissioners, submit a final report to the minister in such form and with such details as the minister may direct-
So far as I know as yet there has been no report, and I would ask the minister whether he has required the commission to make one. They have been sitting now for several months, and even an interim report would help this committee a great deal in dealing with these items. Surely they are not to be passed before we have had the advantage of seeing an interim report by the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I should like to explain to my hon. friend that the item under discussion deals solely with pensioners, that is, those who have acquired a claim on the government because of disabilities incurred on service. I am not for a moment raising a point of order, but whether an interim report or a complete and final report has been received _ from the War Veterans' Assistance Commission will not in any way affect the present item. But I may say to my hon. friend, for his own information, that the commission has been from coast to coast in Canada; it has been in touch with those interested in the problems of returned soldiers in almost every large centre in the country, and it has made certain reports which I shall be prepared to table within the next day or so. But those reports will have no effect whatsoever on the question under discussion. My hon. friend will remember that really the duty of the War Veterans' Assistance Commission was to ascertain approximately the number of ex-service men throughout Canada who were unemployed and what possible means could be found to obtain employment for them.

soldiers have agreed to act on these committees. Certain recommendations have come to us, for instance one dealing with a corps of commissionaires. The recommendation has been approved by the department and will be tabled within a day or so. Another recommendation dealing with a community centre in one section of the country has also been approved. But I think my hon. friend will agree that to say that there is any general panacea for settling unemployment among returned soldiers at the present time would be almost ridiculous. We must handle the situation as best we can in each locality, with the help of the best minds available who have agreed to help us, and that is what we are doing. I do not expect the final report of the commission for some time to come. They have been barely able to classify the reports which they have received. I may say this, that 33,000 returned soldiers filed replies to the questionnaires, which, I take it, means that there are 33,000 returned soldiers out of employment. How many of these are pensioners at the present time and receive a small allowance and relief I am unable to say, because the figures have not been placed before me. But there will be no information disclosed by that committee which will have any great effect on the vote now before us for European war pensions, because most of those who are to be dealt with by the committee will be people who obviously have no claim for pensions, and are not claiming for them. The very large proportion are persons who are asking that they be given some kind of dole or gratuity because they served in the army. So far no government in Canada has been willing to accept the principle that service alone shall entitle a person to payment or to treatment different from that accorded to any other section of the community.
Claims and representations of which I know unofficially have been made to the committee to the effect that because an ex-soldier who is in receipt of a pension gets a minimum relief of $18.75, that, therefore, an ex-imperial soldier who came into Canada in 1928 or 1929 and who is in receipt of $12 or $13 from his municipality should receive the same amount of money. If that claim is made it will possibly be placed very energetically and strenuously before parliament.

I am giving an extreme case.
I want that understood. A large number of ex-imperial troops came to Canada after 1924. Prior to 1924 we had treated them on exactly the same basis as the Canadian soldier. A large number of them were men who commuted or sold their pensions. That is to say they are not in receipt of one dollar from their own government. However, owing to the fact that the legislation of that day provided that if they were here before 1924 they should be placed on the same basis as Canadian soldiers, we pay them the full amount of $18.75 if single men, and running up to $60 or $70 and even to $80 if they are married men, depending upon the number of children they have.

The claim now being made upon us, which is in fact urged in hundreds of cases, is that those who came here since 1924 should be placed in exactly the same position. I do not know whether I speak for the government or not, but certainly I speak for myself when I say that I would not be prepared to recommend to this committee that we assume the obligation of any other government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Unless there is a reciprocal arrangement. We have that with New Zealand.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Perhaps this is not the time to say so, but I did make representations along those lines and I was told very frankly, perhaps too frankly, that the British government considered that they should make no distinction among their pensioners. If their pensioners in England were to be treated in such a way, there was no particular reason why they should treat their pensioners in Canada in another way. Whether this parliament or the people of Canada wish to take in everyone who has served in any army of the British Empire and immediately put him on some kind of dole or relief, making a distinction between him and the ordinary average civilian which should not exist unless he has been wounded, or unless he has some war disability, is for parliament or the people to say. If that condition arises, then the whole policy of various governments since the war will have to be revised.

As I have said, so far we have taken into consideration those who have incurred disability. We have presumed disabilities for those who were burned out. We have gone to the length of making certain payments to those who have a fairly strong claim on this small country, and I doubt very much, when all the facts are placed before it, whether parliament will be willing to adopt the principle of immediately saying that anyone who wore a uniform in any part of the British Empire-and if we take the British Empire we may as well include the allies-will immediately be placed on some special kind of dole or some special kind of pension which will distinguish him from his fellow citizens.
So far no legitimate soldiers' organization has urged anything in this connection, and I doubt very much whether for some time to come they will urge it. I repeat, however, that in spite of that something will have to be done for those who are no longer able to obtain employment. I doubt very much whether we shall do it by a system of general hand-outs, such as I have just indicated, but something certainly will have to be done. It will be the duty of this parliament to work out the problem in a manner satisfactory to the Canadian people.

So, after considerable discussion with the officers of the department we agreed upon a program for enlarging our present study of child and maternal welfare. It will also give us an opportunity, not to overlap provincial work on industrial hygiene, but of doing what a great many provincial ministers of health asked us to do,, of making studies which they require. For instance, there has arisen in this country and in the republic to the south of us a great demand for a further knowledge of silicosis. So far that has been looked after entirely by the provinces, and I know that Ontario in particular has specialized in its studies of that particular disease, and has been, I understand, fairly successful. But if a certain amount further were granted it would be possible for the federal department to give what the doctors are fond of calling " leadership in health " in respect to certain industrial diseases which are common to all the provinces.
There has also been made the suggestion that there should be more publicity and health education undertaken by the department itself. I notice that my right hon. friend shakes his head.

I am not yet firmly convinced one way or the other, but I do believe that in the hands of the department, publicity and health education would be a great boon to Canada, rather than leaving that work to individual associations throughout the country whose activities are controlled largely by their own particular interpretation of the purposes for which grants were extended.
The provinces, when consulted, requested that they have available with us consultants on industrial hygiene, child and maternal welfare, epidemiology, and so on and so forth, and it is for that reason that these increases are being asked for this year.
I hope the committee will give us an opportunity of bringing back this Department of Health to the status which it was originally intended to have, that of the leading Department of Health in the Dominion of Canada.
At the present time, owing to financial circumstances, the depression and one thing and another, the Department of Health is simply, if I may speak in military terms, a skeleton corps, and if we are to do something that will be of benefit to the country as a whole I think the department should be strengthened.

It is an international convention long ago entered into between the United States and Canada. There will also be an assistant chief, laboratory of hygiene; one senior bacteriologist, one senior laboratory assistant, and one laboratory assistant, making a total of $51,580.

speechtext: So far as the federal department is concerned, my hon. friend will understand that we cannot very well quarantine a province. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It is surprising to me, as
one who has been engaged in public health activities in this province for a period of twenty-five years, to see any display of levity with reference to the expansion of the health activities of the federal government. I remember reading a short time ago that the leader
XMr. Stewart.]
of the opposition, in moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne twenty-five years ago, suggested that a federal department of health should be established in Canada. Such a department was established shortly after that time and for a few years I believe there was considerable interest in the matters to which it devoted its attention. During a succession of years following the federal department of health came to be known to the people of Canada more because of its inactivity than because of anything it had ever done. It is, therefore, a matter of congratulation to the present minister that he contemplates at this time expanding the Department of Health.
The medical profession throughout the country, and particularly those who are engaged in public health matters, look to the federal department for leadership, but they have not been getting it under either Liberal or Conservative administration throughout the last decade. It is little wonder that the ministers of health of the several provinces come to the federal government and ask for an appropriation for work to be carried on in those provinces when that work should be done by the federal government itself through its Department of Health. I wonder whether it is the policy of the minister to carry on these new activities through departments which he will inaugurate and have directly under his supervision, or whether he intends to make grants to voluntary agencies who have been more or less doing that work.
Canada owes to the voluntary agencies who have been doing public health work a great debt of gratitude. They have been doing pioneer work in public health, aided by very meagre grants from the federal department. The department of child welfare received last year, I believe, a grant of $13,000. For some reason or another that department, which was formerly carried on under a trained medical man at its head, was transferred to an agency presided over by a lay person. The work in maternal welfare and public health education has fallen down very materially, and the best evidence of that is shown right in the city of Ottawa, which has the highest infant mortality rate of any city in the dominion. Here, under the very shadow of parliament hill, where the people should be given leadership in public health education and in maternal and child welfare, there is a mortality rate which leads the whole country. That is a reflection upon the Department of Health as far as health education goes. The department and the government, it is true, have given recognition at times to men who

Supply-Pensions and National Health
have done something in the sphere of preventive medicine. We make a grant annually to Sir Frederick Banting in recognition of his discovery. Could not something be done to stimulate research in Canada along preventive medical lines? Could we not have a department of national medical research just as we have a department of scientific research? I believe that if we had such a department many of the ills to which the people of Canada are heirs would be coped with successfully, and not only would that accrue to the health of the people, but we would reap the economic benefit as we went along.
Does the committee realize that at any time in Canada there are 180,000 people on the sick list, and that the economic loss to the country is in the neighbourhood of $300,000,000 per annum? Yet what are we doing about it? So far as the federal government is concerned practically nothing is being done. Nothing is being done by the Department of Health in connection with research in cancer, in diabetes, in heart disease, all of which are leading causes of death and disability. I believe it was Disraeli who said that the health of the nation should be the prime concern of any minister, and that holds good to-day just as it did in Disraeli's time. Health is wealth; and if the Department of Health has as its first consideration, as it should have, the health of the nation, then it will extend its activities a great deal further even than is proposed under this additional set-up. I must commend the minister for at least taking a step forward in the direction of preventive medicine.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should not like to detract one iota from the remarks which have just been made, but at the same time I feel that this additional item is adding an extra burden to the already over-burdened ratepayer in Canada. We have health work actively carried on in our schools and school districts. We have health work of the same nature as suggested by the minister carried on by private agencies. We have active health work, as suggested by the minister in connection with this item, carried on by the various municipalities throughout Canada. We have in each and every province of this dominion a department of health actively carrying on aggressive educational work. Over and above that we have a Department of Health in connection with the dominion government. There is a considerable degree of overlapping despite what has been said previously in this committee. There is overlapping not only as between federal and other agencies, but as between the various agencies which exist in the different provinces.
I cannot agree to the passing of this item without registering a protest, for I feel that it is in the estimates for the sole purpose of providing more, and more lucrative, positions for friends and those kindly disposed towards the present government. I do not like to make a suggestion of that kind, particularly in connection with a department presided over by so genial and congenial a minister as we have at the present time, but at the same time I should be remiss in my duty to my electors and to the taxpayers of Canada if I did not voice a sentiment that immediately arose in my mind when I saw this additional item in the estimates. I may be wrong; I may be stating a thought which does not exist in the minister's mind, but it does exist in mine. If this work were not carried on in the provinces and the various municipalities I would certainly agree to this addition. If the minister could give us some assurance that at this conference which was held with the provincial representatives they had agreed to curtail their activities and in that way lessen the burden of expense on the provinces in order to have that work done by the dominion government more effectively than it can be done by the provinces, by all means let us agree to this increase. But sufficient work has been carried on in this field. There is too much overlapping. We should do away with the overlapping and overexpenditure as a result of it, before we increase an item of this kind. I should like to have some assurance from the minister that that is in prospect, so that the taxpayers of this country will recognize that we in this parliament are not adding $52,000 to the amount of money required to be collected without some compensation, or some elimination of overlapping and resultant overexpenditure. The Canadian people are already overtaxed, and I feel that every minister should make it his purpose, if at all possible commensurate with the work required to be done, to reduce taxation, to lessen the burden thereof, so that the people of Canada will feel that the government are at any rate striving to make a step in the direction of lightening their burden during these rather distressful times.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am quite willing to give my hon. friend the assurance that as far as the federal department is concerned there is no intention of undertaking any service which is now being carried on by any provincial department. And I can assure him further that my understanding with the provincial ministers of health was that they

wished the federal department to go into this field because they themselves could not afford to do so. It is a new field entirely.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Would the minister state exactly what is that new field which is covered by this particular item of $52,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Such provinces as the
three prairie provinces, and possibly the maritimes, would like certain services made available by this government because they cannot afford to carry them on at present; I refer to such matters as child and maternal welfare, epidemiology, industrial hygiene and public health education. The larger provinces, such as Quebec and Ontario, carry on certain of these services, I think, but we shall not be establishing anything in the way of a new branch which will overlap work done by the provinces or cause any extra expenditure of money.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: According to the statement of the minister then, there will be a certain amount of overlapping in connection with Ontario and Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No; we shall be doing different work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: My understanding was that the federal department was going to do work which is being done in Ontario and Quebec but not in the smaller provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Ontario and Quebec possibly may not need these services which we are proposing to establish; they may have the facilities to carry them on themselves, and I have no doubt they have the necessary funds. But they have no objection to our carrying them on and having consultants to be of assistance to the other provinces. I hardly think it likely that Saskatchewan would feel able to go to Quebec and Ontario with the same assurance that it could go to a federal department to consult about or ask for assistance for work which can be done by that province.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to have heard from the minister a statement something like this; that as a result of this conference the provinces have agreed to discontinue work in such and such fields, and consequent upon that I am asking for an extra grant of $52,000. We have sitting in this committee at the present time the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley). No doubt he could tell us how difficult it is to collect a sufficient amount of taxes even to approach a balanced budget. And he could relate many instances of the difficulties he experienced during the past year in attempting to collect taxes to

meet our expenditures. We should try to make his work lighter, as well as bearing in mind the unfortunate taxpayers. I should like to have a definite assurance from the minister that that is the case; that the provincial authorities are actually withdrawing from a certain field and that we can thus hope for lessened expenditure in that department as far as the provincial governments are concerned. Then the taxpayers of Canada as a whole will see that their taxes are not actually being increased by this increased expenditure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I desire to make a few observations about this matter, especially in view of the statement just made by the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann). It is quite true that some twenty-five years ago I advocated the establishment of the Department of National Health. It is equally true that I still believe it has a distinctive and responsible work to discharge.
But health is a little different from almost any other branch of governmental endeavour. Primarily we have the advantage of all the work that is done, for instance, by the Rockefeller Institute, by the great Carnegie foundations and by all the other countries in the world. That becomes available at once to the people of the Dominion of Canada, and our poverty stands in the way of our carrying on research work to anything like the degree to which that work is carried on in other countries. A moment ago the minister mentioned the expenditure of a sum of money for the purpose of further investigating a disease which arises out of the working of quartz-silicosis. Down in South Africa I had occasion to look into that for a very special reason. There they are carrying on gold mining operations at a depth of from eight thousand to ten thousand feet. Johannesburg itself is six thousand feet above sea level, and the loss of life which came about through the inroads of this disease was such that action had to be taken. Already they have devised methods by which they have entirely eliminated the risk, by dampening the faces of the working areas, so that they are no longer threatened with any disease from that cause. They, of course, compelled the great enterprises that were carrying on these operations to contribute very largely in order to attain this end.
All that information is available to us without the necessity of setting up a department. We can get it without difficulty. It is quite true, as the minister says, that there is reluctance on the part of people to apply to other governments for information, but on

Sup-ply-Pensions and National Health
the other hand there is always an avowed willingness on the part of the governments of the British Empire to communicate with one another. It will be remembered that not long ago an attempt was made to bring about a correlation of the activities of the various countries that comprise the commonwealth in order that information might be readily available to the peoples of the different countries. In this country we have no difficulty in obtaining the benefit of the tremendous amount of work that is done in the United States by the great enterprises and research bureaus to which I have referred.
Let us be fair when we talk about the federal department. Doctors have frequently said that the federal department has been a failure, but the federal Department of Health never came into being, as the minister said a moment ago, for the purpose of carrying on work in connection with mental hygiene or problems of that sort. It was rather to be a clearing house through which the information obtained in world wide activity might be made available to the various provinces to assist them in discharging their constitutional functions. If difficulties have arisen by reason of impoverishment and lack of revenue to enable the provinces to carry on this work, then another situation entirely arises which is absolutely foreign to the matter we now have under consideration.
Let us take this as a practical question; let us start with the schools. Who provides medical attention in the schools now? I wonder if it is realized that in almost every part of Canada, certainly in every province so far as I know, provision is made for medical inspection and services for the children who attend the schools. In the cities and towns that is well provided for. In the rural municipalities the situation is much more difficult, and just how to get over the difficulty is a matter that, to my knowledge, has engaged the attention of the provincial authorities in some of the remote communities for a very, very long time. But you do not suggest that the federal government should give leadership with respect to a matter of that kind. It would be idle to say that the Department of Health in Canada should take from the provincial departments of health and the municipalities control over all these matters What would be the result? A moment ago the minister referred to Ontario. I recall investigating for my own information the situation in that province in connection, for instance, with the dental clinic. There was travelling over that province a dental clinic looking after the teeth of school children.
In New Brunswick the Red Cross clinic was travelling over the province giving free dental service to those who required it. I was one of the executive officers of that organization at the time, and I was amazed at the condition of the teeth of the children as indicated by the reports which were made by that travelling clinic. The other day in New Zealand I saw twenty-five or thirty children around the age of twelve or thirteen going into a clinic in the city of Wellington for the purpose of having their teeth examined and "stopped" as they call it there, consequent upon decay. That work was being carried on under a centralized government. In that country they have a million and a half people and everything rests with the central authority. But if you say to some of the provinces-I will not name them, because I fancy they are fairly well known; I have had experience, and I speak in the light of that experience-that you are prepared to take over that work, they will tell you they do not want the federal government meddling in their purely local and domestic matters. That has been the attitude in regard to provincial rights in this dominion. Is it suggested that the federal department should undertake duties of that kind? I think the minister has already answered that question; he does not suggest it for a moment. On the contrary, as I understand him he thinks the department does not exist for that purpose at all.
We are starting with the children. You have the clinic in the school; you have the health of the child being carefully looked after. Then you go into the great realm of contagious and infectious diseases. Under our constitution the quarantining, the putting up of notices, the making of investigations- I am leaving out for the moment ships and sailors-rest entirely with the provinces. They carry on that work. Is it suggested that the federal government should undertake that class of work? I think not.
Then you go a step further; you have the great voluntary organizations to which the minister referred a moment ago, and by the movement of my head, perhaps consequent upon a long voyage, I did not intend to negative in any sense the suggestion that the minister was making; quite the contrary. We have the great voluntary organizations, such as the Victorian Order of Nurses. I fancy everyone of us -makes contributions to that order every year, and it carries on a very, very excellent work. Then you have the Red Cross hospitals in outlying sections, that are looking after the people in those areas. Then you have many of the provinces developing what are called municipal

hospitals, through unions of municipalities, which care for the people within those areas. The difficulties, of course, lie in the matter of cost. In these days of impoverishment they have not the money with which to maintain hospitals, and they are not provided with funds for the purpose of paying the dues which may accrue when their people may have to go to other hospitals.
Then you have introduced into the subject matter another factor which owes its origin to one of the great insurance companies of the world. That company conceived the idea of extending the length of human life, 'believing that by doing so through the care of their policyholders they would secure additional funds in the way of premiums for two, three, four, five, six, eight or ten years. Those additional funds would 'become available as part of their capital with which to meet claims under their policies, and they 'believed that by utilizing a portion of their moneys they would be able to find a balance on the right side if the portion was thus used foi the purpose of ensuring the health of their policyholders. That has developed to a tremendous extent. Free medical examination of .the policyholders has been provided. In the .policy of at least one company of which I know, with some fifty million policies outstanding, there is a provision which authorizes the agent of the company to visit the home, and there is a travelling nurse who from week to week goes from home to home of the policyholders for .the purpose of endeavouring to improve the health of the people.	[DOT]
Those are voluntary organizations. Add to them the great national organizations carrying on research work. The hon. member for Renfrew South says that the federal government should give a lead with respect to, let us say, cancer research. Well, Mr. Chairman, when you think of the enormous sums of money being spent annually in the British Empire in connection with research work, and the opportunities that are afforded Canadian research workers in those laboratories to give the best that is in them, the question of setting up here a laboratory for the purpose of research work in cancer is one which I think the minister would consider worthy of very careful consideration, before taking action in connection with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There is the matter of duplication.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Precisely; because it is the kind of effort the results of which are immediately made available to all. That was the reason why a British Empire cancer

research bureau was set up, the idea being that in one particular line of research the work might be carried on in New Zealand, in another it might be carried on in Canada, and in another in Australia. The centralized effort would be at some spot such as London, or some other place which might be selected for the purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The bureau even made
grants to Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
As a matter of fact the minister knows what has been done in some countries. I saw certain research workers in Dunedin, New Zealand, carrying on research work in connection with one phase of the work. I happen to know something of the work which is being done in London in correlating and coordinating these various activities. I do not think the hon. member will suggest that the Dominion of Canada should endeavour to utilize the taxpayers' money to set up a great research bureau, especially in view of the munificent-I use the word deliberately-the munificent gifts of some Canadians in connection with British Empire cancer research. I believe one citizen in the city of Montreal gave a hundred1 thousand dollars in that cause.
At the jubilee of His late Majesty we in Canada endeavoured to create a cancer research fund. The response to it was not as generous as might have been expected, but the province of Saskatchewan, where there was suffering from crop failure, subscribed small contributions extending over wide areas, and the total was large, having regard to their condition. The fund is not large at the moment; I believe it is only a few hundred thousand dollars. What is a few hundred thousand dollars in a work of that kind? It is nothing. When we think of the vast sums that are available in the Rockefeller Institute or the Carnegie foundation or in some other of the foundations, the vast sums which have been set aside and endowed for this purpose, I think we must agree that at this time it is not quite fair to suggest that the federal Department of Health is lacking in leadership simply because it does not establish a great research bureau for cancer or other research work. Having regard to these difficulties, and the willingness of our citizens to make contributions to every work, wherever it may be possible. I do not think that duty rests upon the taxpayers of Canada.
Then we come into the realm of infectious and contagious diseases. The provinces are carrying on a good work in that connection. I say to the minister that I still believe he can accomplish more good work by educa-

Supply-Pensions and National Health
tional process under the direction of the government itself than through these organizations. Much, of course, may be said for them, but it is a fact that the organizations which receive these sums of money by way of grants in aid must necessarily use a great part of the money to maintain their organizations and to pay salaries.
The extent to which the work of the department may 'be extended is one which each minister will have to settle for himself. The minister in the late government made provision whereby he would bring together a meeting of nurses and doctors, various members of hospital boards, government officials and others interested in health, to try to arrive at a point where a national policy under the control of the minister might function, if one may use that word with respect to a policy. That must be done without in any sense impinging upon the activities of the provinces. That is the problem to which the minister has given his attention. He says: I am going to have another sanitary engineer; I will pay $5,000 in salaries, and a few hundred dollars for a few clerks. That would be sound, if it were based upon the assumption that it would not be impinging upon the work carried on by the provincial authorities.
In other words the ministry of health as I conceive it, and as I have always conceived it, is primarily one for the dissemination of knowledge, and one which may assist in the work which may be carried on for the purpose of eradicating disease. In other words it must assist preventive medicine. One of the finest addresses in recent years on the question of preventive medicine was delivered by the late Lord Moulton at Leeds university. The question of preventive medicine he there discussed is one which has engaged the attention of public men during all these years. I for one will entirely support the minister in any effort he may make to assist preventive medicine, but the assistance of preventive medicine, as a policy, must be carried into effect without impinging upon the work being done by the provinces in that connection. We cannot get into the field of the work the provinces are doing; I have in mind dental work and work in connection with infectious diseases.
In the question of research we must realize the problem is one of our ability to provide facilities, having regard to the fact that knowledge acquired in one part of our world is in a very short time available in other parts. For instance, Sir Frederick Banting did not sell his discovery; he made it available, and as a result we find insulin available in all parts of the world for the purpose of accomplishing the ends for which it is used. The research work carried on by a private individual resulted in a great discovery. The Connaught laboratories in Toronto are carrying on a good work in vaccines and serums. A short time ago I visited a laboratory outside Pretoria in which the same work is being carried on on a large scale. The large amount of money that is being spent is not altogether for the relief of humans, but has some connection with the matter of food and that of veterinary services. All the knowledge obtained in Germany, in France and in Canada was lying in the laboratory I visited, available to all concerned. Having regard to the knowledge available to Canadians I do not think we can ibe blamed for not giving leadership, such as is so frequently suggested should be given by the Department of National Health. We have not embarked upon an extensive scheme of that kind. Unless the situation is entirely changed through the surrender of control by the provinces, I believe the federal department can carry on its work only as a disseminator of knowledge obtained through world effort for the purpose of coping with and preventing disease.
I was abused for my views when I was in office, and perhaps I shall be abused for what I say to-night, but I still believe the minister can utilize the machinery of government to disseminate knowledge and to bring it home to the minds of the people of Canada much more readily than by taking a sum of money and handing it over to a particular person. That is my conviction. I may be all wrong, but that is my view with respect to it, and I shall support the minister in any effort he may make in that connection.
The welfare work to which the hon. member for Renfrew South referred is entrusted to an organization under lay leadership. It is quite true that that was done by arrangement and agreement between the government and the organization which is supported by the contributions of insurance companies and other institutions. There is also the aid given by this government. So far as my observations lead me to conclude anything, that work was well done and was deserving of the confidence of the government and the people of this country.
However, do not let us believe that the Department of National Health has not done anything. That department has endeavoured to do at least three things. First, it has to do with the activities and responsibilities which rest entirely with the federal government. Second, it has endeavoured to foster such efforts on the part of the provinces as will assist them to the utmost in carrying on their
Supply-A griculture

campaign in connection with preventive medicine and enable them to oope with disease. Third, it has made efforts toward publicity *and toward making known to the people the necessity for hygiene, good air, cleanliness and all these matters that have to do with public health. I think within the financial1 limits at its disposal this department has accomplished a great deal.
In England the department of public health can deal with these matters because there is no provincial jurisdiction. They do it, but they do not impinge upon the work carried on by the cities and towns. They only lay down the broad principles upon which the work is to be carried on. Wherever you have a unitary system of government, such as there is in New Zealand and other parts of the world, it is very simple for the central power to carry on its health operations. However, where you have a federal union in which jurisdiction is not only held but exercised by provinces or states, in order to deal with these problems there must be a surrender of those powers to the central government before that government can undertake expenditures. Otherwise there would be a duplication of the work and the citizens of the country would be called upon to pay twice for the same services. I think that is axiomatic.
That is the difficulty I have always experienced in dealing with the matter. Unless the provinces have changed their minds during the last few months, they are not willing or prepared to surrender their jurisdiction to the federal power even though the federal power were willing to undertake this work in its entirety, which I do not think any federal government is anxious to do. The very nature of the work lends itself to local administration much better than it does to centralized authority in a country such as this.
I think the minister is to be commended for his efforts to accomplish the purposes he has referred to this evening. I notice the usual grants are being made this year, so the matter need not be further discussed at this moment. Apparently he has concluded that he should stick to the old custom and because of long precedent support the private enterprises which are carrying on this work. However, I think this work could be better carried on either by the provinces or by the dominion. I have not seen anything in what I have read-I have not had the opportunity to read everything-which would indicate that the provinces1 are willing to surrender their jurisdiction in order that this w'ork might be carried on by the dominion. Until that happens, the federal power must necessarily be exercised to the best of its ability. While there may be lacking that spectacular leadership to 
which reference has been made, it must be Temembered that we are but 11,000,000 people. But we are the heirs to all the knowledge that has been accumulated and is being secured by varying investigations and researches in various countries.
